stages.place: Road trip: Kyoto prefecture to Kobe

sumimasen.why: Your most useful word. It gets a waiter's attention, apologises, and even thanks someone for a small favour. Calling すみません! across a restaurant is normal, not rude.

hai.why: Also means 'I'm listening' or 'here you go'. People say it constantly just to show they're following.

iie.why: Correct but blunt on its own. You'll soon learn softer ways to turn things down.

arigatou.why: Casual on its own. The う at the end just stretches the お sound: a-ri-ga-too.

gozaimasu.why: A very polite 'there is'. It attaches to set phrases to raise the politeness: ありがとう ございます.

onegaishimasu.why: お (polite) + ねがい (a wish) + します (I do): 'I make a request'. Name the thing you want, then add this.

konnichiwa.why: The daytime greeting. The last は is said 'wa' because it began life as the topic marker: 'as for today...'

ohayou.why: Add ございます to make it polite, which you should with staff and strangers.

konbanwa.why: Same build as こんにちは: こんばん (this evening) + は, said 'wa'.

douzo.why: You'll hear it when someone offers you a seat, a menu or the way through a door.

kore.why: Something near you. Point at the menu and say これ.

sore.why: The thing near the person you're talking to, like a dish on their side of the counter.

are.why: Away from both of you. これ, それ, あれ: the first sound tells you how far away it is.

wa.why: Marks what the sentence is about, like 'as for...'. Written は but said 'wa' in this job.

nan.why: The question word 'what'. It sits where the answer would go.

desu.why: The polite 'it is'. Always at the very end. The u is almost silent: 'dess'.

ka.why: Add か to the end and any sentence becomes a question. The word order never changes.

niku.why: Useful for checking what's in a dish.

sakana.why: Fish is everywhere in Japanese food, including the stock.

yasai.why: You'll need this one for the vegetarian in your group.

takoyaki.why: Osaka's street food: たこ (octopus) + やき (grilled). やき shows up in lots of dish names.

sou.why: そう です means 'that's right'. You'll confirm things with it all day.

chigaimasu.why: Literally 'it differs'. A polite way to say 'no, that's wrong' without a blunt いいえ.

n4.why: Also read し, but よん is the safe everyday choice.

n7.why: Also read しち. なな is clearer and never misheard as いち.

n9.why: Also read く in a few set words such as くじ (9 o'clock).

n10.why: After ten, numbers stack: じゅういち is 11, にじゅう is 20.

hitori.why: People are counted with にん, but one and two are irregular.

futari.why: The second irregular one. From three onward it's just number + にん.

yonin.why: Careful: よにん, not よんにん.

rokunin.why: ろく (six) + にん (people). Your group's number.

o.why: Marks the thing being acted on. Written を, said 'o'. It points back at the word before it: 'this is the thing I mean'.

kudasai.why: A direct, polite 'give me'. おねがいします is a touch softer. Both are fine in any restaurant.

hitotsu.why: The general counter for things. It works for nearly anything on a menu.

mittsu.why: The small っ is a tiny pause: mit-tsu.

muttsu.why: One each for your whole group.

biiru.why: The long line ー stretches the vowel before it: bii-ru.

omizu.why: お (polite) + みず (water). Free water is normal in restaurants.

ocha.why: お (polite) + ちゃ (tea). Usually green, and often free.

karaage.why: An izakaya staple that everyone orders.

edamame.why: えだ (branch) + まめ (bean). A safe vegetarian starter.

to.why: Joins nouns: A と B. Only for things, not for joining sentences.

mo.why: Takes the place of は or を to mean 'too'.

watashi.why: Japanese drops 'I' whenever it's obvious, so you'll use this less than you expect.

haibooru.why: Whisky and soda. On every izakaya menu.

remonsawaa.why: Shochu, soda and lemon. The other izakaya classic.

uuroncha.why: The standard non-alcoholic order at an izakaya.

gohan.why: Means cooked rice, and by extension a meal.

yakitori.why: やき (grilled) + とり (bird). The same やき as in たこやき.

okonomiyaki.why: おこのみ (as you like it) + やき (grilled). Osaka's savoury pancake.

toriaezu.why: 'For now'. とりあえず ビール is such a common opener it's practically a proverb.

ijou.why: Signals the end of your order.

mou.why: Adds 'one more': もう いちど is 'one more time', もう ひとつ is 'one more'.

yukkuri.why: Also means 'relaxed'. Staff may say ごゆっくり: 'take your time'.

wakarimasu.why: Polite verbs end in ます.

wakarimasen.why: ます becomes ません and the verb turns negative.

wakarimashita.why: ます becomes ました for the past: 'I have understood'. Use it to accept what you've been told.

sukoshi.why: Softens anything: すこし わかります.

chotto.why: The casual twin of すこし. Said alone with a trailing voice, ちょっと... is how people say no without saying no.

madamada.why: The modest reply to any compliment: 'still a long way to go'.

doko.why: Same family as これ: ここ, そこ, あそこ, and the question form どこ.

toire.why: Katakana is for borrowed words, so sounding it out often gives you the English.

eki.why: Train station. The place name goes first: きょうとえき.

migi.why: You'll hear this in almost every set of directions.

hidari.why: Japan drives on the left, same as home.

massugu.why: The small っ is a tiny pause: mas-sugu.

konbini.why: Short for 'convenience'. Open all hours, with ATMs, food and toilets.

hoteru.why: Japanese has no separate l sound, so 'l' becomes る.

arimasu.why: For things. Add か to ask 'do you have...?'

arimasen.why: The same ます to ません swap you already know.

imasu.why: The partner of あります, used for people and animals.

ga.why: Marks the thing that exists or does something. よやく が あります: 'a booking exists'.

no.why: Links two nouns, with the describing one first: えいご の メニュー is 'English menu'.

menyuu.why: Small ュ joins the sound before it: nyu.

seki.why: Staff say おせき. In Japanese you ask for seats, not a table.

namae.why: Staff say おなまえ when asking for yours.

waifai.why: Small ァ joins フ to make 'fa'.

hyaku.why: Changes sound in three places: さんびゃく (300), ろっぴゃく (600), はっぴゃく (800).

sen.why: Changes in two places: さんぜん (3,000) and はっせん (8,000).

man.why: Japanese counts in ten-thousands: いちまん is 10,000, にまん is 20,000.

de.why: Marks the means: カード で is 'by card'. Later you'll see it mark where an action happens.

genkin.why: Still needed at small shops, rural petrol stations and some ryokan.

daijoubu.why: 'All right'. X は だいじょうぶ です is also the polite 'no thanks'.

fukuro.why: Shops charge for bags, so the clerk will ask.

okaikei.why: お (polite) + かいけい (accounts). Crossing your index fingers in an X means the same thing.

betsubetsu.why: Not every place will split the bill, so asking is polite.

zenbu.why: ぜんぶ で is 'for everything, in total'.

suika.why: The tap-and-go transit card. It also pays at konbini and vending machines.

gochisousama.why: Said as you finish or leave. ごちそう means 'a feast', and でした is the past of です: 'it was a feast'.

ikimasu.why: Also covers 'will go'. Japanese has no separate future tense.

kaerimasu.why: Going back to where you belong: home, or your hotel.

ikimasen.why: The same ます to ません swap as わかりません.

ni.why: Marks a destination: きょうと に いきます. It also marks a point in time, and where something is.

kyouto.why: The old capital. きょう (capital) + と (city).

oosaka.why: Two お in a row make one long 'oo'.

toukyou.why: とう (east) + きょう (capital). Both vowels are long: too-kyoo.

kyou.why: Sounds the same as the きょう in きょうと, but it's a different word.

ashita.why: Time words like this need no particle.

takushii.why: The doors open and close by themselves, so don't touch them.

kono.why: これ stands alone. この must be followed by a noun: この バス.

tsugi.why: You'll hear it in every train announcement.

yoji.why: Irregular: よじ, not よんじ.

shichiji.why: Irregular: しちじ, not ななじ.

kuji.why: Irregular: くじ, not きゅうじ.

han.why: Goes after the hour: しちじ はん is 7:30.

kara.why: Goes after the starting point, in time or place.

made.why: The partner of から. In a taxi, place + まで is 'to'.

mise.why: Covers anywhere that sells things, including places to eat.

tabemasu.why: A regular verb: every form is built by swapping ます.

nomimasu.why: Also used for taking medicine and for soup.

shimasu.why: The all-purpose verb. Noun + します makes hundreds of verbs, as in レンタル します.

nani.why: The same word as なん. It's なん before です, and なに before を and が.

osake.why: Means alcohol in general as well as sake itself.

raamen.why: Every region has its own style.

itadakimasu.why: Literally 'I humbly receive'. Said before the first bite. Its partner at the end is ごちそうさまでした.

tabemashita.why: ます becomes ました for the past.

ikimasendeshita.why: Negative past: ません plus でした.

mou2.why: The same もう as 'more'. With a past verb it means 'already'.

mada.why: まだ です on its own means 'not yet'.

otera.why: Buddhist. Kyoto has well over a thousand.

jinja.why: Shinto. Look for the gate at the entrance.

hajimete.why: X は はじめて です: 'it's my first time in X'.

oishii.why: The word you'll use most at the table.

atsui.why: Used for both hot weather and hot things.

samui.why: For weather and how you feel, not for cold drinks.

ii.why: The one irregular adjective: its other forms start with よ.

takakunai.why: Drop い, add くない.

oishikatta.why: Drop い, add かった.

yokatta.why: The past of いい. Also said with relief: 'thank goodness'.

suki.why: Works like an adjective: X が すき です is 'I like X'. The u is nearly silent: 'ski'.

nigate.why: A gentle way to say you don't like something or can't handle it.

kirei.why: Ends in い but is a な-adjective.

nigiyaka.why: A compliment for a busy street or restaurant.

na.why: な-adjectives need な before a noun: きれい な おてら.

ne.why: Invites agreement. It makes a statement friendly instead of flat.

ja.why: じゃ ありません is the negative of です.

ikitai.why: Swap ます for たい.

ikitakunai.why: たい words change like い-adjectives: たい becomes たくない.

oshiro.why: Osaka and Himeji both have famous ones.

omiyage.why: Bringing gifts back is close to a duty in Japan, so every station sells them.

ikimashou.why: Swap ます for ましょう.

sorosoro.why: A soft way to suggest wrapping up.

minna.why: みんな で is 'all together'.

otona.why: On ticket machines and price boards.

dou.why: X は どう ですか: 'how about X?' or 'how is X?'

ichimai.why: まい counts flat things: tickets, plates, shirts.

matte.why: From まちます. Verbs with ち before ます take って.

misete.why: From みせます. Just swap ます for て.

oshiete.why: From おしえます. Covers both telling and teaching.

kaite.why: From かきます. き before ます becomes いて.

totte.why: From とります. り before ます becomes って.

itte.why: From いいます. It sounds the same as 'go' (also いって), and context tells you which.

shashin.why: Small ゃ blends with し: sha.

juusho.why: Show a taxi driver the address on your phone and say この じゅうしょ まで.

tometemo.why: とめて (park) + も. The も is what turns a request into 'even if I...'.

tottemo.why: とって (take) + も. Don't confuse it with とても (very).

dame.why: Direct, but normal for rules. You'll hear it more than you say it.

menkyo.why: You need your home licence and an International Driving Permit together.

kaeshimasu.why: かえります is you going back. かえします is giving a thing back.

regyuraa.why: Standard unleaded, which most rental cars take. The pump handle is red.

mantan.why: まん (full) + タン (tank). Half hiragana, half katakana because 'tank' is borrowed.

etc.why: The card that lets you drive straight through expressway toll gates. Ask the rental desk for one.

serufu.why: Many petrol stations are self-service. Staffed ones will wave you in and ask what you want.

itte2.why: From いきます, the one irregular て-form. Sounds the same as 'say'.

shingou.why: Directions in Japan count traffic lights, not street names.

chuushajou.why: ちゅうしゃ (parking) + じょう (place).

juppun.why: ふん becomes ぷん after a small っ.

gurai.why: Goes after the amount: いちじかん ぐらい.

kousoku.why: Short for こうそくどうろ. Tolled, with green signs.

mayoimashita.why: Past of まよいます. みち に まよいました: 'I lost my way'.

chekkuin.why: The small ッ is a tiny pause: chek-kuin.

azukatte.why: From あずかります: to hold something for someone.

ippaku.why: Nights are counted with はく, which becomes ぱく here.

yukata.why: The cotton robe the ryokan gives you. Wear it to dinner and to the bath, left side over right.

osewa.why: おせわ に なります literally means 'I will be in your care'.

narimasu.why: Also the shop-polite ending you heard in prices: に なります.

ofuro.why: In Japan you wash first, outside the tub, then soak.

otokoyu.why: おとこ (man) + ゆ (hot water). Usually behind a blue curtain.

onnayu.why: おんな (woman) + ゆ (hot water). Usually behind a red curtain.

kashikiri.why: A かしきり bath is one you book for your own group. Handy for mixed groups and couples.

dekimasu.why: Noun + できますか asks whether something is possible.

tsukaemasu.why: The 'can' form of つかいます (use).

ikkai.why: Japan counts the ground floor as the first floor.

nikai.why: One floor up from the ground.

nuki.why: Goes after the thing to leave out: にんにく ぬき.

bejitarian.why: Understood, but often taken to mean 'no meat' only. Spell out fish and stock too.

tamanegi.why: たま (ball) + ねぎ: the round onion.

negi.why: A separate word from たまねぎ, and sprinkled on almost everything. Name both if both are a problem.

dashi.why: The base of most soups and sauces, usually made from fish flakes. The hidden problem for vegetarians in Japan.

haitteimasu.why: A set form for now. Lesson 27 explains the ています ending.

taberaremasen.why: The 'can't' form of たべます. Clearer for dietary needs than たべません, which sounds like a preference.

osusume.why: Staff like being asked, and you often get the best dish.

ryouri.why: やさい の りょうり: vegetable dishes.

rentaru.why: レンタル します is 'to rent'.

buutsu.why: Boot sizes in Japan are in centimetres.

uea.why: Jacket and trousers. Small ェ joins ウ to make 'we'.

senchi.why: Used for boot size and your height.

choudo.why: ちょうど いい: 'just right'.

ichinichi.why: Days have their own words up to ten.

yokka.why: Don't mix it up with ようか, which is eight days.

kan.why: Added to days to stress a duration: よっか かん is 'for four days'.

yuki.why: Niseko gets around fifteen metres of it a season.

futteimasu.why: From ふります, used for rain and snow.

gondora.why: The first thing to close when the wind picks up.

rifutoken.why: けん means ticket or pass.

ichinichiken.why: いちにち (one day) + けん (pass).

itai.why: An い-adjective. Body part + が いたい です.

tasukete.why: From たすけます. Shouted alone, it's 'Help!'

byouin.why: Careful: びよういん, with a big よ, is a hair salon.

sumaho.why: Short for スマートフォン.

kouban.why: Small neighbourhood police posts. The place to go for lost property and directions.

kyuukyuusha.why: Dial 119 for an ambulance or fire, 110 for police.

yonde.why: From よびます. び before ます becomes んで.

kega.why: けが を します: 'to get hurt'.

noriba.why: バス のりば, タクシー のりば.

kippu.why: For trains and buses. チケット is for events and attractions.

yuki2.why: Sounds like 'snow', but follows a place name on buses and trains.

takuhaibin.why: Door-to-door delivery. You can send skis or suitcases ahead to your next hotel or the airport, usually overnight.

yamanote.why: Tokyo's loop line. せん means 'line'. Shibuya, Shinjuku and Tokyo Station are all on it.

nanbansen.why: なん (what) + ばん (number) + せん (track).

kaisatsu.why: Where you tap in and out.

norimasu.why: Takes に: でんしゃ に のります.

orimasu.why: Takes で for the place: しぶや で おります.

chaaji.why: From 'charge'. チャージ します is 'to top up'.

ao.why: Also covers the green of traffic lights.

shichaku.why: しちゃく します is 'to try on'.

shitemo.why: して (do) + も, the same permission pattern as とっても.

menzei.why: Shops with the Tax-Free sign take the tax off for visitors. Bring your passport.

purezento.why: Say it and they'll gift-wrap, usually for free.

dake.why: Goes after the word it limits.

miteiru.why: The plain form of みています, used here before だけ.

no2.why: After an adjective, の stands in for the noun: やすい の is 'a cheap one'.

hajimemashite.why: Literally 'for the first time'. Only for a first meeting.

sundeimasu.why: The same ています form: a continuing state.

sundeimashita.why: います becomes いました.

shigoto.why: Asking someone else, make it おしごと.

kaishain.why: The catch-all for anyone employed by a company.

kochira.why: You've heard staff use it for 'this way' and 'this'. It also introduces people politely.

yoroshiku.why: Closes an introduction. With おねがいします it's polite.

tanoshikatta.why: Drop い, add かった.

ichiban.why: いちばん + adjective makes a superlative: いちばん おいしい.

mata.why: また ね is a casual 'see you'.

benkyou.why: べんきょう します is 'to study'.

shiteimasu.why: します in the ています form.

akemashite.why: Used only in the New Year greeting.

omedetou.why: For birthdays and weddings too. Add ございます to be polite.

yoi.why: A more formal form of いい that survives in set phrases.

kanpai.why: Wait until everyone has a drink before the first sip.

hatsumoude.g: first shrine visit of the year
hatsumoude.why: Millions go in the first three days of January. Expect queues, food stalls and a festive mood.

omikuji.why: Drawn at shrines and temples. A bad one gets tied to the rack, to leave the bad luck behind.

toshikoshisoba.why: Eaten on New Year's Eve. The long noodles stand for a long life.

ojamashimasu.why: Literally 'I'm going to be in your way'. Said as you step into someone's home.

otsukaresama.why: Said at the end of a day out, a shift or a ski run. One of the most-used social phrases in Japan.

lessons.can: Greet people, thank them and get a waiter's attention
lessons.point: Politeness in Japanese lives in the endings of words. ございます and します are polite endings you will see everywhere. On sounds: every kana gets one even beat, and う after an お sound just makes it longer.

phrases.kj: ありがとうございます
phrases.note: Use the full version with staff and strangers.

phrases.kj: すみません、お願いします
phrases.en: Excuse me, could I get some help?
phrases.note: How you call staff over to your table.

hear.tip: Every shop shouts it. No reply needed: a nod or こんにちは is plenty.
Follow them to your table.

lessons.k: これ は なん ですか
lessons.can: Ask what something is and check what's in it
lessons.point: A は B です means 'A is B'. Add か and it's a question, with no change in word order. Question words like なん sit where the answer would go.

hear.kj: こちらはたこ焼きです
hear.tip: Staff say こちら where you would say これ.

lessons.can: Ask for a table for two to six
lessons.point: Japanese puts a counter word after the number. For people it's にん: さんにん, よにん, ごにん, ろくにん. One and two are irregular: ひとり, ふたり. Four is よにん, not よんにん.

hear.tip: Answer with your number: ろくにん です.
Staff count guests with めいさま instead of にん. Just say はい.

lessons.k: これ を ふたつ ください
lessons.can: Order any number of anything, even by pointing
lessons.point: を marks the thing you want. The number comes after を, right before the verb: thing を number ください. ひとつ, ふたつ, みっつ is the general counter, and it works for almost anything on a menu.

phrases.kj: これを2つお願いします
phrases.note: おねがいします works anywhere ください does, and sounds a little softer.

hear.kj: ご注文はお決まりですか
hear.en: Have you decided on your order?

hear.tip: What staff say after taking your order.
Said as your food or drinks arrive.

lessons.k: ビール と おみず
lessons.en: And, also, and ordering for the group
lessons.can: Order several different things for six people in one go
lessons.point: と joins nouns: A と B. も takes the place of は or を and means 'too'. Chain them and one sentence can carry a whole table's order.

phrases.kj: ビールとお水をください
phrases.en: A beer and a water, please.

phrases.kj: ビールを3つとハイボールを2つください
phrases.en: Three beers and two highballs, please.

phrases.kj: とりあえずビールを6つください
焼き鳥とお好み焼きをください

hear.tip: A half-sentence: the question is implied.

hear.kj: 以上でよろしいですか
hear.tip: Reply はい、いじょう です.

lessons.can: Keep a conversation going when you get lost
lessons.point: Polite verbs end in ます. Swap it for ません and the verb is negative: わかります becomes わかりません. Swap it for ました and it's past: わかりました. Those three endings work on every verb you'll learn.

phrases.kj: もう一度お願いします
ゆっくりお願いします
すみません、わかりません
ちょっとわかりません
phrases.note: Softer than a flat わかりません.

phrases.kj: 日本語は少しわかります

phrases.en: Not at all, I've a long way to go.

hear.tip: You'll hear this after saying almost anything. The expected reply is the modest まだまだ です.

lessons.k: トイレ は どこ ですか
lessons.can: Ask where anything is and follow the answer
lessons.point: X は どこ ですか works for any place. The answer usually uses the ここ, そこ, あそこ family, or みぎ, ひだり and まっすぐ.

hear.tip: The polite version of あそこ.

hear.kj: まっすぐ行って右です
hear.en: Go straight, and it's on the right.

lessons.can: Ask if they have something, and say you have a booking
lessons.point: あります means 'there is' or 'I have', for things. います is the same for people. が marks the thing that exists. In questions and negatives, は usually takes over: メニュー は ありますか. の links two nouns: えいご の メニュー.

phrases.kj: 英語のメニューはありますか
phrases.en: Do you have an English menu?
There are six of us. Do you have a table?

hear.kj: 申し訳ございません、満席です
hear.tip: Common for a group of six. Reply わかりました、ありがとう ございます and try next door.

lessons.can: Ask a price and understand the answer
lessons.point: Bigger numbers stack like blocks: に + ひゃく is 200, さん + ぜん is 3,000, いち + まん is 10,000. A few change their sound: さんびゃく, ろっぴゃく, はっぴゃく, さんぜん, はっせん. The price game drills these by ear.

phrases.note: Numbers stack: ご + ひゃく.
Ten thousand is いちまん, never じゅうせん.

hear.tip: に なります is the shop-polite way of saying です.

lessons.can: Pay, split the bill, and turn down bags and extras
lessons.point: で marks the means: カード で is 'by card', ぜんぶ で is 'for everything'. だいじょうぶ means 'fine', and X は だいじょうぶ です is the polite way to say 'no thanks'.

phrases.kj: カードでお願いします
カードで大丈夫ですか

phrases.note: Literally 'as for a bag, I'm fine'.
Say it to the staff on your way out.

hear.kj: お会計はご一緒でよろしいですか
hear.tip: Reply はい, or べつべつ で おねがいします.

hear.kj: お席が分かれてもよろしいですか
hear.en: Is it OK if you're seated apart?
hear.tip: Common with six. Reply はい、だいじょうぶ です, or いっしょ で おねがいします.
Reply だいじょうぶ です or おねがいします.
Asked at the konbini. Reply おねがいします or だいじょうぶ です.

hear.kj: ポイントカードはお持ちですか
hear.en: Do you have a point card?
hear.tip: Reply だいじょうぶ です.

lessons.k: きょうと に いきます
lessons.can: Say where you're going and how, and check a bus or train
lessons.point: The verb comes last. ます covers both present and future, so いきます is 'I go' and 'I will go'. に marks the destination and で marks the transport.

phrases.en: I'm going back to the hotel.

phrases.kj: このバスは京都駅に行きますか
phrases.en: Does this bus go to Kyoto Station?

lessons.can: Ask opening hours and meal times, and direct a taxi
lessons.point: Time is number + じ. Three are irregular: よじ (4), しちじ (7), くじ (9). はん adds 'half past'. から is 'from', まで is 'until' or 'as far as', and に marks the time something happens.

phrases.kj: 朝ご飯は何時からですか
この店は何時までですか
phrases.en: What time is this place open until?

phrases.kj: 京都駅までお願いします
phrases.note: The taxi pattern: place + まで + おねがいします.

phrases.en: I'll go at half past seven.

hear.kj: ラストオーダーは9時半です

hear.tip: The taxi driver's opening line.

hear.kj: チェックアウトは11時です

lessons.can: Say what you eat and drink, and what you don't
lessons.point: を marks what the verb acts on. で marks where the action happens: ここ で たべます. To say you don't do something as a rule, use は with the negative: にく は たべません.

phrases.kj: 持ち帰りでお願いします

hear.kj: 店内でお召し上がりですか
hear.tip: Reply ここ で たべます, or もちかえり です.

hear.kj: お飲み物は何にしますか
hear.en: What will you have to drink?

lessons.can: Talk about what you did today or yesterday
lessons.point: ます becomes ました for the past, and ませんでした for the negative past. です becomes でした. There's no separate 'have done' form: もう たべました covers both 'I ate' and 'I've eaten'.

phrases.kj: 昨日大阪に行きました
たこ焼きを食べました
昨日は行きませんでした

phrases.en: It's my first time in Kyoto.

hear.en: Is it your first time in Kyoto?

hear.tip: Reply もう たべました, or まだ です.

lessons.can: Say food is delicious, and that something is too expensive, cold or small
lessons.point: い-adjectives end in い and go straight in front of a noun: おいしい みせ. For the negative, drop い and add くない. For the past, drop い and add かった. です only adds politeness. いい is the one irregular: よくない, よかった.

phrases.kj: おいしい店はありますか
phrases.en: Is there a good place to eat?

hear.tip: Reply とても おいしい です.

hear.kj: 熱いのでお気をつけください
hear.en: It's hot, so please be careful.

lessons.en: Likes, and a second kind of adjective
lessons.can: Say what you like and don't, and admire a view
lessons.point: な-adjectives behave like nouns. They need な before a noun (きれい な おてら), use じゃ ありません for the negative, and でした for the past. が marks the thing you like. ね at the end invites agreement.

phrases.kj: 日本の食べ物が好きです
辛い食べ物は苦手です
phrases.en: I'm not good with spicy food.
It's a beautiful temple, isn't it?

hear.kj: 苦手なものはありますか
hear.en: Is there anything you can't eat?
hear.tip: Restaurants and ryokan often ask this.

lessons.can: Say what you want to do, eat, see and buy
lessons.point: Swap ます for たい and the verb means 'want to'. A たい word then behaves like an い-adjective, so 'don't want to' is たくない. Add です to keep it polite.

phrases.en: I want to go to the castle.

phrases.kj: ラーメンを食べたいです

phrases.en: What do you want to do?

phrases.kj: お土産を買いたいです
トイレに行きたいです
ビールを飲みたいです

phrases.en: I want to see a temple.

phrases.kj: 今日は行きたくないです
phrases.en: I don't want to go today.

hear.kj: どこに行きたいですか
hear.en: Where do you want to go?
What do you want to eat?

lessons.can: Make plans as a group and buy six tickets
lessons.point: ましょう means 'let's'. ませんか is a softer invitation: 'won't you...?' Both hang off the same stem as ます. Flat things such as tickets are counted with まい: いちまい, にまい.

phrases.kj: そろそろ帰りましょう
ビールを飲みませんか
ビールを飲みましょう
タクシーで行きましょう
みんなで食べましょう

lessons.can: Ask people to wait, show you, write it down or take your photo
lessons.point: The て-form plus ください is a polite request. Verbs reach the て-form in a few regular ways. たべます and みせます just swap ます for て. With い, ち or り before ます, it's って: まちます becomes まって. かきます becomes かいて, のみます becomes のんで, します becomes して. いきます is the odd one out: いって.

phrases.kj: ちょっと待ってください
これを見せてください
写真を撮ってください
ここに書いてください
もう一度言ってください
この住所までお願いします
phrases.note: Show the driver your phone as you say it.

hear.kj: こちらにお名前を書いてください
hear.tip: Busy restaurants keep a waiting list at the door. Write your name and the number in your group.

lessons.k: とめても いいですか
lessons.can: Ask whether you can park, take photos, sit or come in
lessons.point: て-form + も いいですか asks permission: literally 'is it good even if I...?' So とって ください asks someone else to take a photo, and とっても いいですか asks whether you may.

phrases.kj: ここに車を止めてもいいですか
写真を撮ってもいいですか
ここに座ってもいいですか
ここで食べてもいいですか

hear.tip: A trailing ちょっと means no. Nobody will say the word 'no'.

lessons.en: Picking up the car, and petrol
lessons.can: Collect your rental car, ask about returning it, and fill the tank
lessons.point: の chains as far as you need: レンタカー の よやく. Notice the pair かえります (go back yourself) and かえします (give a thing back). まで に means 'by' a deadline.

phrases.kj: レンタカーの予約があります
phrases.en: I have a rental car booking.

phrases.kj: 免許とパスポートです
phrases.en: Here are my licence and passport.

phrases.kj: 英語のナビはありますか
phrases.en: Does it have an English sat nav?
Do you have an ETC card?

phrases.kj: 何時までに返しますか
phrases.en: By what time do I return it?

phrases.kj: レギュラー満タンでお願いします
phrases.en: Fill it up with regular, please.

phrases.kj: ガソリンスタンドはどこですか

hear.en: What would you like to do about insurance?

hear.kj: 満タンでお返しください
hear.en: Please return it with a full tank.

hear.tip: Asked at staffed petrol stations.

hear.kj: 現金ですか、カードですか

lessons.can: Ask the way, understand turn-by-turn answers and find parking
lessons.point: Minutes are number + ふん, which becomes ぷん after some numbers: ごふん, じゅっぷん. Hours are number + じかん. ぐらい after an amount means 'about'. In directions, を marks the place you turn at and に marks the direction you turn.

phrases.kj: 車でどのくらいですか
phrases.en: How long is it by car?

hear.kj: 次の信号を右に曲がってください
hear.en: Turn right at the next traffic light.

hear.kj: まっすぐ行ってください

lessons.can: Check in for six, ask about meals and leave your bags
lessons.point: Nights are counted with はく, which shifts to ぱく after some numbers: いっぱく, にはく, さんぱく. で after a number of people means 'as a group of'. Ryokan staff use formal words for meals, ゆうしょく and ちょうしょく, where you'd say ばんごはん and あさごはん.

phrases.kj: チェックインをお願いします
荷物を預かってください
チェックアウトは何時ですか

phrases.note: The classic line on arriving at a ryokan.

phrases.kj: 浴衣は部屋にありますか
phrases.en: Are the yukata in the room?

hear.kj: ご朝食は7時から9時までです
hear.en: Breakfast is from seven to nine.

hear.kj: お部屋にご案内します
hear.en: I'll show you to your room.

lessons.en: Baths, and what you can do
lessons.can: Find the bath, book a private one, and ask if you can use a card or Wi-Fi
lessons.point: できます means 'can do', and noun + できますか asks if something is possible: よやく できますか. つかえます is 'can use'. To say where something is, mark the place with に: へや に あります.

phrases.kj: お風呂は何時までですか
phrases.en: Until what time is the bath open?

phrases.kj: 貸切のお風呂は予約できますか
phrases.en: Can we book the private bath?

phrases.kj: トイレは2階にあります
phrases.en: The toilet is on the second floor.
It's my first time at an onsen.

hear.en: The men's bath is on the second floor.
The women's bath is on the ground floor.

hear.kj: タオルはお部屋にあります
hear.en: The towels are in your room.

hear.kj: 12時までご利用いただけます
hear.en: You can use it until twelve.

lessons.k: にんにく ぬき で
lessons.can: Explain what people in your group can't eat, and ask what's in a dish
lessons.point: X ぬき で orders something without X. が はいっています asks or says what's inside a dish. Kitchens often can't change a dish at short notice, so ask what's in it first, and tell ryokan about dietary needs before you arrive.

phrases.kj: 肉と魚は食べられません
phrases.en: They can't eat meat or fish.

phrases.kj: 魚のだしも食べられません
phrases.en: They can't have fish stock either.

phrases.kj: 友達はにんにくと玉ねぎが食べられません
phrases.en: My friend can't eat garlic or onion.

phrases.kj: にんにくと玉ねぎ抜きでお願いします
これはにんにくが入っていますか
phrases.en: Does this have garlic in it?

phrases.kj: 野菜の料理はありますか
神戸牛を食べたいです
phrases.en: I want to eat Kobe beef.

hear.kj: アレルギーはございますか
hear.tip: Asked at many restaurants and every ryokan. It's your opening to explain.

hear.kj: こちらはにんにくが入っています
hear.en: This one has garlic in it.

hear.kj: 申し訳ございません、できません
hear.en: I'm sorry, we can't do that.

lessons.k: もう すこし おおきい
lessons.can: Rent gear, give your sizes and ask for a better fit
lessons.point: もう すこし + adjective means 'a little more': もう すこし おおきい. Days have their own words up to ten: いちにち, ふつか, みっか, よっか, いつか. Adding かん stresses the length of time.

phrases.kj: スキーをレンタルしたいです
もう少し大きいサイズはありますか
phrases.en: Do you have a slightly bigger size?

phrases.kj: ヘルメットもお願いします

hear.kj: 身長は何センチですか
hear.en: How tall are you in centimetres?

hear.tip: Reply しょしんしゃ, ちゅうきゅう or じょうきゅう, plus です.

hear.kj: こちらにご記入ください

lessons.k: ゆき が ふっています
lessons.can: Talk about the weather and check what's open and running
lessons.point: て-form + います describes something happening now or a state that continues: ふっています (it's snowing), あいています (it's open). You've already met it in はいっています.

phrases.kj: 今日の天気はどうですか
ゴンドラは動いていますか
リフト券を買いたいです
phrases.en: I'd like to buy a lift pass.

phrases.kj: この店は開いていますか
リフトは混んでいますか

hear.tip: The word to catch is うんきゅう.

hear.kj: ゴンドラは止まっています
今日は閉まっています

lessons.can: Say what hurts, report a lost item and get help
lessons.point: Body part + が いたい です says what hurts. なくしました is the past of 'lose'. You hope not to need these lines, so learn them until they come out without thinking.

phrases.kj: スマホをなくしました

phrases.en: I want to go to a hospital.

phrases.kj: 救急車を呼んでください
友達がけがをしました

lessons.can: Find your bus, ask how long it takes and send bags ahead
lessons.point: かかります is 'takes', for time and money: どのくらい かかりますか. A place name + ゆき on a bus or train means 'bound for'.

frames.en: How long does it take to ___?

phrases.kj: バス乗り場はどこですか
次のバスは何時ですか
phrases.en: What time is the next bus?

phrases.kj: 空港までどのくらいかかりますか
phrases.en: How long does it take to the airport?

phrases.kj: このバスはひらふに行きますか
phrases.en: Does this bus go to Hirafu?

phrases.kj: ひらふまで大人1枚お願いします

phrases.en: I'd like to buy a ticket.

phrases.kj: 荷物をホテルに送りたいです
phrases.en: I'd like to send my luggage to the hotel.

phrases.kj: スキーを宅配便で送りたいです
phrases.en: I'd like to send my skis by delivery.

hear.en: It takes about two and a half hours.

hear.kj: 飛行機は遅れています
ひらふ行きは3番乗り場です
hear.en: The bus for Hirafu leaves from stop 3.

lessons.k: しぶや に いきますか
lessons.can: Check your train, find your platform and exit, and top up your card
lessons.point: Trains use three particles. に marks the train you get on (でんしゃ に のります) and where you're headed. で marks the station where something happens (しぶや で おります). Big stations name their exits by compass point, so check which ぐち you need before you tap out.

phrases.kj: この電車は渋谷に行きますか
phrases.en: Does this train go to Shibuya?

phrases.kj: どこで乗り換えますか
Suicaをチャージしたいです
phrases.en: I'd like to top up my Suica.

hear.kj: まもなく2番線に電車が参ります
hear.en: A train will shortly arrive at platform 2.

hear.kj: 山手線はお乗り換えです
hear.en: Change here for the Yamanote Line.

lessons.k: これ に します
lessons.can: Try things on, ask for other colours and sizes, and buy tax-free
lessons.point: X に します means 'I'll go with X', in shops and restaurants alike. の after an adjective means 'one': やすい の is 'a cheaper one'. しても いいですか is the same permission pattern you learned for parking.

phrases.kj: 試着してもいいですか

phrases.en: Do you have it in black?

phrases.kj: もう少し安いのはありますか
phrases.en: Do you have a slightly cheaper one?

hear.tip: Reply みている だけ です.
Reply はい, or プレゼント です to get it wrapped.

hear.kj: 免税カウンターは7階です
hear.en: The tax-free counter is on the 7th floor.

hear.kj: パスポートをお願いします

lessons.can: Introduce yourself and your friends, and say where you're from
lessons.point: すんでいます is the same ています form: 'am living'. Change います to いました and it becomes 'used to live'. Japanese drops 'I' and 'you' when they're obvious, so はじめまして, your name, です is a complete introduction.

phrases.kj: オーストラリアから来ました
東京に1年住んでいました
phrases.en: I lived in Tokyo for a year.

phrases.kj: オーストラリアに住んでいます
よろしくお願いします
phrases.note: Always the last line of an introduction.

hear.en: Is this your first time in Japan?
hear.tip: Your answer: いいえ、とうきょう に いちねん すんでいました.

lessons.can: Keep a friendly chat going and talk about your trip
lessons.point: Good conversation in Japanese is mostly reacting. そう ですね agrees, そう ですか shows interest, ほんとう ですか shows surprise. Use them often and you'll sound engaged even with few words.

phrases.kj: 京都はとてもきれいでした
スキーは楽しかったです
ラーメンが一番好きです
日本語を勉強しています

hear.kj: 何が一番おいしかったですか
hear.en: What was the best thing you ate?

lessons.k: あけまして おめでとう
lessons.can: Say the right thing before and after midnight, toast, and visit a shrine
lessons.point: New Year has a script. Until 31 December you part with よい おとし を. From 1 January it's あけまして おめでとう ございます, always followed by ことし も よろしく おねがいします.

phrases.note: Only up to 31 December. The を trails off with the rest left unsaid.

phrases.kj: 来年もよろしくお願いします
phrases.en: I look forward to next year too.

phrases.kj: 明けましておめでとうございます
今年もよろしくお願いします
phrases.en: I look forward to this year with you too.
phrases.note: Always follows the Happy New Year line.

phrases.kj: これはオーストラリアのお土産です。どうぞ
phrases.en: This is a gift from Australia. Please.

phrases.kj: 年越しそばを食べましょう
phrases.en: Let's eat New Year's Eve soba.
Let's go for the first shrine visit.

phrases.kj: おみくじはいくらですか
phrases.en: How much is a fortune slip?

hear.kj: どうぞ上がってください

hear.tip: The best fortune you can draw.

bosses.role: a server at a busy izakaya in Osaka
bosses.setting: Get a table for your group of six, order drinks and food in the right quantities, and pay.
goals: Say how many people you are
Order at least two different drinks with quantities
Order two dishes
Ask for the bill and say how you'll pay

bosses.role: a ticket seller at a Kyoto temple, and then a taxi driver
bosses.setting: Buy tickets for your group, ask what time it closes, then take a taxi back to your hotel.
goals: Buy the right number of adult tickets
Ask the closing time
Say something about the temple
Tell the taxi driver where to go

bosses.role: the host at a small-town ryokan
bosses.setting: Arrive with your group of six, check in, sort out dinner and food needs, and find the bath.
goals: Check in under your booking name
Confirm how many people and nights
Explain the group's food needs
Ask about dinner time and the bath

bosses.role: a staff member at a ski rental shop in Hirafu
bosses.setting: Rent your gear for the right number of days, sort out sizes, and ask about lift passes and today's conditions.
goals: Say what you want to rent and for how long
Give your boot size and level
Ask for a different size
Ask whether the gondola is running

bosses.role: a friendly local you've just been introduced to at a New Year's Eve gathering in Tokyo
bosses.setting: Introduce yourself, chat about your trip, toast, and get the greetings right on both sides of midnight.
goals: Introduce yourself and say where you're from
Say something about what you did on the trip
React naturally to what they say
Give the right New Year greeting

lessons.can: Read every hiragana again, including the marks and small letters
lessons.point: Hiragana writes native Japanese words and all the grammar. Two marks change a sound: ゛ turns か into が, and ゜ turns は into ぱ. A small ゃ, ゅ or ょ blends with the kana before it (きゃ), and a small っ is a short pause before the next sound.

lessons.can: Sound out menus and signs written in katakana
lessons.point: Katakana writes borrowed words, so sounding one out often gives you the English. The line ー stretches the vowel before it (ビール is bii-ru). Small ァィゥェォ make sounds Japanese didn't have, such as ファ (fa) and ウィ (wi).

signs.where: The polite word, on signs in restaurants and stations
On the curtain at the entrance to a bath
Red upside-down triangle road sign, and painted on the road
Road signs near crossings and narrow streets
Often shortened to a large P
Lit in red at car park entrances
Lit at car park entrances and on taxi dashboards
On car park payment machines and station fare-adjustment machines
On the door of shops and restaurants
Restaurants between lunch and dinner service
Followed by the day of the week the place shuts
Roped-off areas, including out-of-bounds ski terrain
